---
title: "Example: seasonal liver plasticity in a treefrog"
bibliography: ../references.bib
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r library}
library(lagprotest)
```

This article analyzes a real data set with `lagged_protest()` and
`lagged_protest_pairs()`. The question is whether seasonal changes in the
liver of the treefrog *Dendropsophus minutus* track climate within the same
month or with a delay, and whether hepatic modules lead one another.

## The data

`dminutus_liver` holds monthly means of four hepatic modules and of
climate, from April 2016 to March 2017
[@francobelussi2026data; see `?dminutus_liver` for the variables]. Each
element is a matrix with 12 rows (months) and one column per variable.
Climate combines temperature, rainfall and humidity from BR-DWGD
[@xavier2022brdwgd], a drought index from TerraClimate
[@abatzoglou2018terraclimate], UV-B irradiance from glUV
[@beckmann2014gluv] and photoperiod.

```{r data}
sapply(dminutus_liver, dim)
```

The series span exactly one annual cycle, so the phase and cyclic schemes,
which treat the series as periodic with period *n*, apply without
truncation (`period` is not needed). With 12 time points, the power to
detect a lag is limited, and strong autocorrelation would make the phase
scheme somewhat liberal (see
[Choosing a permutation scheme](permutation-schemes.html)); the cyclic
scheme is used below as a conservative check.

## Contemporaneous concordance

Concordance within the same month is the lag-0 PROTEST for every pair of
data sets. With a single lag, the global p-value equals the raw one, and
`lagged_protest_pairs()` adjusts it across the ten pairs (Benjamini–Hochberg
by default):

```{r lag0}
lag0 <- lagged_protest_pairs(dminutus_liver, lags = 0, bidirectional = FALSE,
                             nperm = 9999, seed = 1)
knitr::kable(lag0[, c("x", "y", "m2", "r", "p.value", "p.global.adjusted")],
             digits = 3)
```

Somatic indices and climate were the only pair concordant after the
adjustment. Density and climate had the lowest *m*², yet this concordance
was not distinguishable from that expected between independent seasonal
series, which illustrates why a low *m*² alone is not evidence of
association.

## Lagged concordance

The hypothesized hierarchy has seven directed edges: climate to each of the
four modules, and three links between modules. Each edge is scanned from
−3 to +3 months, so a positive lag means that the first data set leads the
second. The global p-value accounts for the scan within each edge; the
edges are then adjusted within two families of hypotheses, because the four
climate edges ask whether each module responds to the same driver, whereas
the biological edges ask a different question. This section uses the
smallest *m*² as the scan statistic (`stat = "raw"`), as in the analysis
of these data submitted for publication; the next section compares it with
the current default, `stat = "minP"`:

```{r lagged}
climate_edges <- list(c("Climate", "Histochemistry"),
                      c("Climate", "Morphometry"),
                      c("Climate", "Density"),
                      c("Climate", "Somatic"))
module_edges <- list(c("Histochemistry", "Morphometry"),
                     c("Morphometry", "Density"),
                     c("Density", "Somatic"))
climate <- lagged_protest_pairs(dminutus_liver, pairs = climate_edges,
                                lags = 0:3, nperm = 9999, seed = 1,
                                stat = "raw")
modules <- lagged_protest_pairs(dminutus_liver, pairs = module_edges,
                                lags = 0:3, nperm = 9999, seed = 1,
                                stat = "raw")
cols <- c("x", "y", "optimal_lag", "n", "m2", "r", "p.value", "p.global",
          "p.global.adjusted", "effect_lag", "Z", "A")
knitr::kable(climate[, cols], digits = 3)
knitr::kable(modules[, cols], digits = 3)
```

Climate led histochemistry by three months, and this was the only edge
whose global p-value remained below 0.05 after adjustment within its
family. Notice the difference between the raw p-value at the optimal lag
and the global p-value: for climate and somatic indices, the raw p-value at
lag 0 was below 0.01, but the global p-value, which accounts for having
chosen the best of seven lags, was not significant. The contemporaneous
test above, which examines a single lag, is the appropriate one for that
pair.

The lag profile of the climate–histochemistry edge shows the minimum at
lag +3:

```{r profile, fig.alt = "Procrustes m2 against lag from -3 to 3 for climate and histochemistry; the minimum, circled and filled, is at lag 3, with global p = 0.011."}
fit <- attr(climate, "fits")[["Climate -> Histochemistry"]]
plot(fit)
knitr::kable(fit$profile, digits = 3)
```

The cyclic scheme gives a conservative check. With 12 rows and
`mirror = TRUE`, its smallest attainable p-value is 1/23 = 0.043, so a
global p-value at that bound is as strong as the scheme can show:

```{r cyclic}
cyc <- lagged_protest(dminutus_liver$Climate, dminutus_liver$Histochemistry,
                      lags = 0:3, bidirectional = TRUE,
                      permutation = "cyclic", stat = "raw")
cyc$p.global
```

## Sensitivity to the scan statistic

The global p-value compares the observed smallest *m*² across lags with
the smallest *m*² of each surrogate. This test is valid, but it does not
weigh all lags equally: under the null hypothesis, *m*² is smaller and
more variable when fewer rows overlap, so the raw minimum tends to fall at
the longest lags. With 12 rows and lags from −3 to +3, the best lag falls
at ±3 in about half of the series simulated by
`simulate_lagged_series()` without association, rather than
in two of seven, and the test has more power for a true lag of three
months than for a contemporaneous association. An edge whose best lag lies
at the end of the scan should therefore be checked with a statistic that
places all lags on the same null scale.

Two such statistics are available through the argument `stat` and can
also be computed from the surrogates stored in each fit, without new
permutations, as done below: the smallest per-lag p-value across lags
(minP), and the smallest standardized *m*², in which the *m*² at each lag
is centered and scaled by the mean and standard deviation of its own null
distribution [@westfall1993resampling]. The observed and the permuted values
are scored in the same way: each permuted *m*² is converted to a p-value by
its rank among all values at that lag, and standardized against the other
values, so that the observed result is exchangeable with the permutations
under the null. Taking the smallest p-value across
tests in each randomization follows the procedure described by
@manly2020randomization [pp. 83--84] for correlated tests, for which the
Bonferroni level is too strict; they recommend at least 100*m*
randomizations for *m* tests, a condition met here by 9999 permutations for
seven lags. The standardized *m*² at each lag is also returned, with the
opposite sign, as `z` in `fit$profile`, and its largest value gives the
effect lag (`effect_lag` in the tables above); the function below adds the
corresponding global p-values:

```{r balanced}
balanced_p <- function(fit) {
  # Observed m2 in the first row, permuted values below; every value is
  # scored in the same way within its lag.
  all <- rbind(fit$profile$m2, do.call(cbind, fit$null))
  n1 <- nrow(all)
  loo_z <- function(v) {  # each value against the mean and SD of the others
    m <- (sum(v) - v) / (n1 - 1)
    s2 <- (sum(v^2) - v^2 - (n1 - 1) * m^2) / (n1 - 2)
    (v - m) / sqrt(s2)
  }
  z <- apply(all, 2, loo_z)
  p <- apply(all, 2, rank, ties.method = "max") / n1
  glob <- function(S) mean(apply(S, 1, min) <= min(S[1, ]))
  c(z = glob(z), minP = glob(p))
}
fits <- c(attr(climate, "fits"), attr(modules, "fits"))
sens <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(fits, balanced_p)))
family <- rep(c("climate", "modules"), c(nrow(climate), nrow(modules)))
sens$z.adjusted <- ave(sens$z, family, FUN = p.adjust, method = "BH")
sens$minP.adjusted <- ave(sens$minP, family, FUN = p.adjust, method = "BH")
knitr::kable(sens, digits = 3)
```

The optimal lag of every edge is the same under the three statistics,
because they differ only in how the lags are compared under the null. The
support for each edge, however, changes. The climate–histochemistry delay
weakens to a global p-value just above 0.05 and does not remain
significant after adjustment within its family, whereas the edges with
their best fit at lag 0 or ±1 gain support. With either balanced
statistic, no edge remains significant after adjustment.

## Reading the results

The analysis points to a delayed response of liver histochemistry to
seasonal climate, of about three months, and to a contemporaneous
association between climate and somatic condition. The delay is the
strongest lead–lag signal in these data, but its significance depends on
the raw statistic, which favors long lags, so it is better read as a
hypothesis for a longer series than as an established timescale. The other edges were not
distinguishable from chance with 12 monthly samples, which does not show
that they are absent: one annual cycle gives little power for weak or
delayed associations, and the optimal lag of a non-significant edge should
not be interpreted. Because the lag is estimated from a single year, it
also describes this cycle rather than a general property of the species.
